title: Diode Effect in Nonlinear High-Kinetic-Inductance Transmission Line Resonators
authors: Niklas Gaiser, Ciprian Padurariu, Björn Kubala, Nadav Katz, Joachim Ankerhold
abstract: High-kinetic-inductance (HKI) transmission lines provide a promising platform for compact nonlinear superconducting microwave devices. Existing theoretical descriptions are typically based on the slowly varying envelope approximation, which becomes inadequate for strongly nonlinear resonant structures with pronounced spatial field variations. Here, we develop a theoretical framework for single-frequency nonlinear wave propagation in HKI transmission lines by formulating the problem as a boundary value problem that retains the full spatial dependence of the electromagnetic fields. Applying the method to resonant transmission-line geometries, we demonstrate power-dependent resonance shifts, bistable transmission solutions, and strongly direction-dependent transport arising from asymmetric impedance barriers, yielding transmission contrasts of up to $93\%$ without magnetic bias fields. The framework is further extended to a three-port stub geometry, where nonlinear interference produces shifted anti-resonances and Duffing-like spectral distortions. Our approach provides a versatile tool for the analysis and design of strongly nonlinear superconducting microwave devices.
summary: This work develops a rigorous theoretical framework using boundary value problems to analyze nonlinear microwave propagation in superconducting HKI transmission lines. By retaining full spatial field dependence, the authors predict strong directionality (diode effect) and complex spectral features like bistability and anti-resonance shifts purely from structural asymmetry. This provides a versatile tool for designing next-generation nonlinear superconducting microwave components.
main_problem: To develop a theoretical framework for nonlinear wave propagation in High-Kinetic-Inductance (HKI) transmission lines that remains accurate even when spatial field variations are strong, overcoming the limitations of the slowly varying envelope approximation.
main_result: The authors demonstrated power-dependent resonance shifts, bistable solutions, and significant direction-dependent transport (diode effect) in superconducting microwave resonators without external magnetic biasing fields.
method: The problem is formulated as a boundary value problem (BVP), allowing for the retention of full spatial field dependence, which is solved using advanced numerical techniques like the shooting method.
model_or_system: The system involves nonlinear HKI superconducting microwave resonators modeled by incorporating a nonlinear inductance per unit length into the telegrapher's equations. The analysis extends to multi-segment and stub geometries.
key_observables: Power-dependent resonance shifts, bistable transmission solutions, direction-dependent transport contrast (up to 93%), and Duffing-like spectral distortions in anti-resonances.
important_parameters:
The nonlinearity is governed by the kinetic inductance term; key regimes include moderate power ($P \ll Z I_*^2$) and structural asymmetry between impedance segments ($Z_1 
eq Z_2$).
main_assumptions: The initial analysis uses a harmonic balance ansatz, assuming higher harmonics are negligible, although the full BVP approach mitigates this limitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic layouts of nonlinear resonators and stub geometries; spectral plots compare $S_{21}$ vs $S_{12}$ to show directionality, and power response curves demonstrate bistability.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the necessity of a full spatial boundary value problem over envelope approximations. It then applies this framework to analyze two-port scattering (showing diode effects) and extends it to multi-segment and stub geometries to explore complex nonlinear interference patterns.
why_interesting: While focused on superconducting circuits, the methodology—developing a robust BVP approach for strongly nonlinear wave equations with spatial dependence—is highly relevant to modeling non-linear dynamics in open quantum systems or photonic structures where boundary conditions are critical.
